intro: Every tree on this list arrived with somebody. Monkeypod only reached Hawaii in the 1840s, and the two thickest of them on the island's register stand behind a shopkeeper's store and in the front yard of a missionary house. The men of a governor of Kauai planted a banyan for him in the 1880s that now measures close to twenty metres round. A plantation owner emptied his leftover nursery stock along a mile of road and made a tunnel out of it. There is an African baobab behind a church in Koloa.
meta_description: Kauai's remarkable trees all arrived with somebody: a shopkeeper's monkeypod, a governor's banyan twenty metres round, and a mile of eucalyptus.
question_answer: The oldest tree on Kauai that anybody can actually date is the Kanoa Banyan at Niumalu, planted for Paul P. Kanoa, governor of the island, at some point in his 1882 to 1886 term, which makes it about 140 years old. It stands roughly 84 feet east of Hulemanu Road on the way down to the Menehune Fishpond, and its trunk and root mass together measure close to twenty metres round, the largest figure recorded for any tree on Kauai in the state's exceptional trees register.
question_meta: The Kanoa Banyan at Niumalu, planted for a governor of Kauai in the 1880s, is the island's oldest datable tree. Where it stands and what is near it.
question_context: Kauai has no thousand-year-old trees, and the dates explain why: the island's designated trees are overwhelmingly species people carried here, and the oldest of them went into the ground during the sugar era. The Kanoa Banyan has the firmest window of any of them. The Garden Island, the local paper, records that it was planted by the men of Paul P. Kanoa, governor of Kauai from 1882 to 1886, in his honour and on his own land, that it still flourishes at Niumalu, and that Kauai County declared it an exceptional tree in 1990 at the request of the family who owned the property by then. That puts it at roughly 140 years. One tree could in principle beat it and cannot prove it: the monkeypod at the Gulick-Rowell House in Waimea, which local tradition dates to 200 years, a figure that fails because monkeypod is generally recorded as arriving in Hawaii around 1847. The Wilcox Banyan at Nawiliwili is the documented runner-up, planted in 1895.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree on Kauai?
faq.a: The Kanoa Banyan at Niumalu, planted for Governor Paul P. Kanoa during his 1882 to 1886 term, so about 140 years old. The monkeypod at the Gulick-Rowell House in Waimea may well be older, but nobody has dated it.

faq.q: Can you walk the Tree Tunnel on Maluhia Road?
faq.a: There is a shoulder and it is narrow. Maluhia Road is the main way between the highway and the south shore, so most people take the canopy slowly by car or by bike. It runs for the better part of a mile.

faq.q: Are these trees free to visit?
faq.a: All of them. They stand on public roads, in a church yard, in Old Koloa Town and on the grounds of a resort at Nawiliwili. The Gulick-Rowell House in Waimea is closed for restoration, but its monkeypod fills the front yard and is in full view from Huakai Road.

faq.q: What did Hurricane Iniki do to them?
faq.a: Iniki crossed Kauai in 1992 and stripped the Tree Tunnel on Maluhia Road back to bare branches. Residents said it would come back, and within a few years it had. The eucalyptus standing there now are the same trees, not a replanting.

trees.name: The Yamamoto Monkeypod

location.address: 5330 Koloa Road, Koloa, HI 96756 (behind the former Yamamoto Store site, Waikomo Stream side)

trees.story:
The man who planted this tree ran the shop in front of it. Howard Yamamoto's family took over the Koloa general store in the early 1920s, and he put a monkeypod in the ground on the Waikomo Stream side of the building, back when the water was still called Koloa Stream. The trunk now measures just under seven metres round, and the county register, which lists it as an exceptional tree, rates its condition as good.

The store it shades was built in 1898 and rebuilt in 1983, so the tree has already outlived one version of the building it was planted behind. It is the shade in the yard where Old Koloa Town does its business, and it has been that since the shop was still a shop.

Its age is the one thing the sources argue about. The store's own history dates the planting to the early 1920s, which makes the tree about a hundred years old. A tourist photography site says 130 and confuses it with a famous monkeypod on Oahu, which is a different tree on a different island. We have gone with the store, on the grounds that the store was there.
trees.access: Free, standing in the open courtyard/streetside area of Old Koloa Town behind the historic Yamamoto Store building. Hurricane Lowell brought down many trees on Kauai in September 2026, and we have no word on this one since, so check it is standing before you make a special trip.
trees.transport: In Old Koloa Town, walkable from anywhere on Koloa Road
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, just under 7 metres round, shading the yard behind the old Yamamoto Store. It stands on the Waikomo Stream side of the building in Old Koloa Town.

trees.name: The Koloa Baobab

location.address: Koloa Missionary Church, 3370 Poipu Road, Koloa, HI 96756 (behind the church yard, near the southeast corner)

trees.story:
A baobab is not what anybody expects to find behind a church in Hawaii. This one stands near the southeast corner of the yard at Koloa Missionary Church, and it sits on the county's register of exceptional trees, which records its condition as excellent and then stops. No girth, no assessment date, no planting record. The register does not even fix the species: it lists the tree as Adansonia, the baobab genus, without saying which baobab it is.

You will not mistake it for anything else. The genus carries an enormous swollen trunk and a crown of thin branches that look like roots held up in the air, which is worth the short walk over from the rest of Old Koloa Town on its own.

The most recent independent confirmation we could find is from 2016, when the Outdoor Circle featured it in a series on favourite trees. That is a long gap for a tree we are sending people to, and the pin marks the church rather than the trunk, because the register's coordinate is a grid point rather than a position. If you have stood in front of it lately, or you know which baobab it is or who put it there, tell us.

trees.name: The Kanoa Banyan Tree

location.address: Niumalu, along Hulemanu Road on the way to the Menehune (Alekoko) Fishpond, approximately 84 feet east of Hulemanu Road

trees.story:
Twenty metres round is not a normal measurement for a tree. This banyan comes to 19.87 at the county's assessment, the largest figure recorded against any Kauai entry in the exceptional trees register, and it gets there the way banyans do: by dropping aerial roots that thicken into extra trunks until one tree becomes a grove of itself. Height 64 feet, condition excellent.

It was planted for a politician. The men of Paul P. Kanoa, governor of Kauai from 1882 to 1886, put it in on his own land in his honour, which makes the tree about 140 years old and the oldest on this list anybody can actually date. The property later passed to the Achi family, and in 1990, at their request, Kauai County declared it exceptional. The island's newspaper looked in on it again this year and reported that it still flourishes.

It stands roughly 84 feet east of Hulemanu Road, on the way down to the Menehune Fishpond, and that sentence is as precise as the record gets. The register describes rather than plots, so our pin marks the road and not the trunk. In practice that is enough. Look for the largest thing in sight.

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, nearly twenty metres round, with aerial roots thickened into extra trunks. It stands about 84 feet east of Hulemanu Road, the largest thing on the way down to the fishpond.

trees.name: The Wilcox Banyan Tree

location.address: Banyan Harbor Resort, 3411 Wilcox Road, Lihue (Nawiliwili), HI 96766, on the former Papalinahoa Road descending from Kuhiau Ridge

trees.story:
The road this tree was planted beside no longer exists. George N. Wilcox of Grove Farm put it in in 1895 on a curve of the Papalinahoa Road, which came down off Kuhiau Ridge to Nawiliwili. The tree stayed and the road went. What grew up around it instead is the Banyan Harbor Resort, so it now spends its days on the grounds of a working condo complex rather than in a park. The drive in is open and the tree is impossible to miss, but go knowing that this is somebody's address.

By the local paper's account it covers about two acres and has put down more than a thousand aerial roots. Its height is genuinely disputed and nobody has reconciled the figures: the county register recorded 38 feet, the newspaper says about 110. The trunk measurement they agree on is 6.58 metres.

Kauai County declared it an exceptional tree in 1976, after the cultural guardian Sarah Kailikea argued its case. The same newspaper column that told its story in 2013 went back to it this year and found it still flourishing. That makes 130 years, in the course of which its road vanished and a resort was built around it.

trees.name: The Tree Tunnel (Maluhia Road)

location.address: Maluhia Road, from Knudsen Gap northward for about 3/4 mile toward Koloa, Kauai

trees.story:
In 1992 Hurricane Iniki took every leaf off this mile of road and left a corridor of bare poles. Residents said it would grow back. Within a few years it had, and the canopy over Maluhia Road today is those same trees rather than a replanting.

There are more than 500 of them, swamp mahogany eucalyptus, standing along both sides of the road that runs from Knudsen Gap up toward Koloa and closing overhead for about three quarters of a mile. Kauai County has recognised the tunnel since 1976, as one thing rather than as 500 things, which is also how anybody driving through it experiences the place.

Who planted it is not settled. The version you will hear most often credits Walter Duncan McBryde, said to have run leftover nursery stock from his Kukuiolono estate down the lane around 1911. A competing local account credits the Knudsen family, planting to firm up a marshy track and break the wind coming across it. Nobody has produced a document that closes the argument, so both are worth knowing.

It is the gateway to the south shore, which means it is a working road. The shoulder is narrow. Most people take it slowly and look up.
verified_sources: Hawaii Exceptional Trees register (data.honolulu.gov, CC0), register_id 1138
trees.access: Free, a public road; drive or walk under the canopy (there is a narrow shoulder, most people experience it from a car or bike). Hurricane Lowell brought down many trees on Kauai in September 2026, and we have no word on this one since, so check it is standing before you make a special trip.

trees.name: The Gulick-Rowell Monkeypod

location.address: Gulick-Rowell House, 9567 Huakai Road, Waimea, HI 96796

trees.story:
Local tradition says this monkeypod is 200 years old and arrived as a gift from an Indian prince, the first of its kind planted on the Garden Isle. The arithmetic does not hold. Monkeypod is generally recorded as reaching Hawaii around 1847, which is 179 years ago, so a 200-year-old specimen would predate its own species' arrival by two decades. It is a fine story about the tree and a poor fact about its age, which is why the age field here is empty.

What is measured is the trunk: 8.53 metres round, the largest monkeypod figure on Kauai in the exceptional trees register, holding up a crown that covers the entire front yard of the Gulick-Rowell House.

The house is the reason the address matters. Reverend Peter Johnson Gulick began building it in 1829 and Reverend George Rowell finished it by 1846, and the restoration project now working on it calls it the oldest house on Kauai. It is closed while that work goes on. The tree is in full view from Huakai Road, and the pin marks where to stand. Wood from one pruned limb has already been made into tables at Kokee Lodge.

Nobody has dated it. If you know who put it in, tell us.

The tree fills the yard and is in full view from the public road; the pin marks where to stand. Hurricane Lowell brought down many trees on Kauai in September 2026, and we have no word on this one since, so check it is standing before you make a special trip.

trees.name: The Allerton Jurassic Park Figs

location.address: Allerton Garden, Lawai Valley (tours depart from the NTBG visitor centre, 4425 Lawai Rd, Koloa, HI 96756)

trees.access: Paid guided tour only, the Allerton Garden Guided Tour (adults $65, children 2 to 12 $32.50, about 2.5 hours, Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday; prices rise in January 2027). Every tour includes a bus ride into the garden. Book ahead and arrive 30 minutes early.
trees.transport: About 25 minutes by car from Lihue to the NTBG visitor centre on Lawai Road, where tours depart.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the buttress roots, rising like walls tall enough to walk between. They stand inside Allerton Garden, where the tour guide points out the spot used for Jurassic Park's raptor-egg scene.
trees.verify_notes: Owner/manager of the ground (National Tropical Botanical Garden) names the Moreton Bay figs and their towering roots as a highlight and cites Jurassic Park. Ensemble not a single named specimen; one place to stand on the tour. Garden Island 2015 (Ryan Kazmirzack): Jurassic Park shot in Allerton Garden in 1992; most recognisable scene has Dr Alan Grant finding raptor eggs among distinctive roots of a Moreton Bay fig; 'so-called Jurassic Park trees' are a popular draw. No planting date, girth or height for these figs found in any fetched page; age left empty. Garden itself created from 1938 by Robert Allerton and John Gregg Allerton (Wikipedia); that is the garden's date, not these trees'. Pin is the NTBG visitor centre / McBryde side; Allerton valley with the figs is roughly 1 km south, exact fig spot unverified (no OSM node checked). ALIVE: NTBG tour page current (pricing notice for Jan 2027) and lists the figs; no tree-specific recent observation. Hurricane Lowell hit Kauai 2026-09-08 with islandwide tree damage; found no report on the figs, so alive-now thin: flagged. Single credible source (owner of the ground) plus one press item. Photo pass 2026-11-04 (approved): Commons file titled Jurassic Park trees of Allerton Gardens, National Tropical Botanical Garden, Kauai; the buttress-rooted figs fill the frame, daylight.
trees.story:
In Jurassic Park, Dr Alan Grant finds a clutch of raptor eggs among the roots of a giant tree. The tree is real, and it is one of the Moreton Bay figs in Allerton Garden on Kauai's south shore.

The Garden Island, the island's paper, recorded in 2015 that the film was shot here in 1992 and that the egg scene, its most recognisable moment in the garden, was filmed among the distinctive roots of a Moreton Bay fig. The garden's managers, the National Tropical Botanical Garden, still lead with them, promising the towering roots of the famous figs from the blockbuster. Locally they are simply the Jurassic Park trees.

What makes them screen-worthy is the buttressing. These figs stand on roots that rise out of the ground as towering walls, tall enough to walk between, and the guide stops among them to show where the scene was shot.

The garden itself was made from 1938 by Robert Allerton and John Gregg Allerton. That is the garden's date, not necessarily the trees', and nobody has published a planting date, girth or height for the figs. If you know when they went in, tell us.

Two honest cautions. Allerton is seen only on a paid guided tour, which starts with a bus ride into the valley. And Hurricane Lowell hit Kauai on 8 September 2026 with damage to trees across the island; we have found no report on these figs either way, so check with the garden before you book.

trees.name: The Poipu Road Earpod

location.address: In front of Borthwick Kauai Mortuary, 3168 Poipu Road, Koloa, HI 96756

location_site.name: Borthwick Kauai Mortuary frontage, Poipu Road

trees.access: Free to see from Poipu Road; the tree stands on the frontage of a funeral home in Koloa town. Keep to the roadside, and stay away during services.
trees.transport: About 20 minutes by car from Lihue to Old Koloa Town.

official_register.name: Hawaii Exceptional Trees register (Hawaii DLNR, via data.honolulu.gov), no. 1137

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the very large spreading tree in front of the Borthwick Kauai Mortuary on Poipu Road, Old Koloa Town. If the register is right, its seed pods are coiled into the shape of an ear.
trees.verify_notes: SPECIES CONFLICT, kept in the story: Hawaii Exceptional Trees register 1137 says Earpod (Enterolobium cyclocarpum); Mayor Bryan Baptiste's letter (The Garden Island, 24 Dec 2007) calls the tree on the Borthwick Mortuary property a monkeypod (Samanea saman). Species follows the register; the story names both and asks the reader to check the pods. Register: girth 725.4 cm, height 54 ft, vitality Excellent, no assessment date, locality 'In Koloa along Poipu Road in front of the Kauai Mortuary, Inc.'. Mortuary street number 3168 from a search result only. No tree-level observation after Hurricane Lowell (2026-09-08). No age basis; Kauai forest-reserve plantings of the species 1926-1935 are a class fact, not bridged.
trees.story:
Two official records agree that the big tree outside the Koloa funeral home is exceptional, and they disagree about what it is. Hawaii's exceptional trees register files it as an earpod. In 2007 Kauai's mayor, writing in The Garden Island, listed the monkeypod tree on the Borthwick Mortuary property among four south-shore trees on the county's exceptional list.

Both cannot be right, and the confusion is an easy one to make. Earpod and monkeypod are close relatives and often mistaken for each other. This page follows the register, which measured the tree, and leaves the question open. The way to settle it is the seed pods. An earpod's pods coil round on themselves into the shape of an ear, which is where the name comes from. If you stand under it and find pods of another shape, tell us, and send a photograph.

The register's figures are 7.25 metres round and 16.5 metres tall, and it rated the tree's vitality excellent. It gives no assessment date, so those numbers are as of some unknown visit.

The tree stands on the Poipu Road frontage of the mortuary in Old Koloa Town, in full view of the road. Nobody has dated it. Hurricane Lowell crossed south Kauai on 8 September 2026 and we have seen no report on this tree since, so if you pass, a sighting helps too. Please keep to the roadside when a service is on.

trees.name: The Hongwanji Monkeypods

location.address: Honpa Hongwanji Mission / Koloa Early School parcel (TMK 2-8-004:056), Old Koloa Town, Koloa, HI 96756

trees.access: Free to see from the public street. The trees stand on a shared Buddhist mission and preschool parcel; look from the road, as the preschool grounds are not open to the public.
trees.transport: About 20 minutes by car from Lihue to Old Koloa Town.

official_register.name: Hawaii Exceptional Trees register (Hawaii DLNR, via data.honolulu.gov), nos. 1151 and 1152

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as a pair of large monkeypods side by side, broad flat-topped crowns of about the same size. They stand on the Honpa Hongwanji Mission and Koloa Early School lot in Old Koloa Town.

(1) Register rows 1151 (girth 490.7 cm, 42 ft = 12.8 m, vitality Fair) and 1152 (girth 457.2 cm, 40 ft = 12.2 m, Fair), both TMK 2-8-004:056, locality 'Old Koloa Town, Honpa Hongwanji Mission and Koloa Early School'. Folded as one pair (twins metres apart per register wording; registers 1151, 1152). Register heights/girths are at assessment, undated. Access: temple grounds are allowed under the rule, but the preschool shares the lot and I could not establish the exact boundary; whether the trunks stand on the Mission side or the preschool side is NOT verified. Pin = Old Koloa Town centre, not the trees. ALIVE: only the 2008 article and register; no recent observation; Hurricane Lowell (2026-09-08) struck south Kauai. Vitality only Fair. Recommend ship only if flagged and access line kept as given. 1150 (TMK 053, girth 487.7 cm, Excellent) is a neighbouring parcel monkeypod, not part of this pair: kept as a lead.
trees.story:
A Buddhist mission and a preschool share these two monkeypods, and in 2008 both said yes to having them protected. The Garden Island reported in June that year that Kauai's Arborist Advisory Committee had recommended adding a pair of monkeypods in Old Koloa Town to the county's exceptional tree list, calling them ideal specimens of older monkeypod trees on location, size and aesthetic quality. The joint owners, the Honpa Hongwanji Mission and Koloa Early School, raised no objection.

The state register now carries them as two entries on the same parcel. One is 4.91 metres round and 12.8 metres tall, the other 4.57 metres round and 12.2 metres tall, close enough in size to read as a matched pair. From the street they read as two broad, flat-topped crowns side by side.

Two cautions belong with them. The register rates both in only fair condition, and it gives no date for that assessment. And Hurricane Lowell crossed south Kauai on 8 September 2026; we have seen no report on these trees since. A visitor's photograph would settle more than any document can.

The parcel is a working preschool as well as a mission, and no source says on which side of that shared lot the trunks stand, so look from the street rather than walking in. Nobody has dated them either. If you know when they were planted, tell us.
